item.title: Bernie Sanders unveils his plan to push Medicare for All when Democrats take power
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation’s healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities. Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, is currently the ranking member on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and is expected to become its chairman when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. His agenda, first provided to The Associated Press, lays out the legislative implementation for proposals that he and progressive candidates championed on the campaign trail this cycle. At the center is Sanders’ longstanding push for Medicare for All , a universal healthcare system that would be implemented over four years. The first year would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guarantee healthcare to children through age 18. “This is no longer a utopian vision. This is where the American people are,” Sanders said in an interview with the AP. The proposals offer an early glimpse of how progressives hope to shape the Democratic Party’s priorities after an election that delivered the party control of Congress but also exposed competing visions for its future. With the 2028 presidential election already looming, Sanders is seeking to push Democrats toward a populist economic agenda that he argues has gained broader support. “I think the election, in my opinion, was a crying out for fundamental change in the way the government does business and the absolute need to protect a struggling working class,” Sanders said. “I think this is a time to bring about very significant changes in policies so that we can actually improve the lives of working families.” Sanders keeps pushing for Medicare for All Sanders has long championed a single-payer national health insurance program that would replace most private insurance with a federally administered system providing universal coverage. His proposal for the new Congress lays out a four-year transition to that system, beginning with expanding Medicare eligibility and benefits. In the second year, the eligibility age would fall to 45, followed by 35 in the third year, before extending coverage to everyone in the fourth year. “Transforming a system which is 18% of the GDP of America, you don’t do that overnight,” Sanders said of the transitional period. But the costs of lowering Medicare eligibility are likely to lead to massive debate between the two major political parties as the national deficit stands at $2 trillion, or 6.2% of gross domestic product. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that lowering the age of Medicare eligibility to 60 would increase federal budget deficits by $155 billion over the 2026–2031 period. Sanders’ prior proposals to pay for the program shift healthcare financing away from private insurance premiums and toward payroll contributions — including a combination of employer and household premiums, higher taxes on the rich and new taxes on Wall Street and large firms. Sanders also argued that Democrats could pass the first stage of the transition through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain tax and spending legislation to advance through the 100-member Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically required to overcome a filibuster. Democrats will have a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the chamber in 16 years. Along with pushing for greater access to primary care, Sanders says Democrats will push for lower prescription drug costs . A changing political landscape Sanders has previously balanced his progressive ambitions with the realities of governing. During his first stint chairing the HELP Committee from 2023 to 2025, he worked with Republicans on legislation to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to primary care. He also chaired the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, helping advance major Democratic spending priorities. But now, just weeks after the midterms, Sanders is laying out an ambitious agenda that he argues reflects a shift not in his own positions but in voters’ demands for sweeping changes to the healthcare system. He sees signs of that shift among Democratic leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has pledged to get to work “right out of the gate” to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republicans. Jeffries said Tuesday that Democrats know that simply returning to the status quo “is not acceptable” and they are preparing ways to further expand healthcare access by lowering the Medicare eligibility age, adding access to vision, hearing and dental coverage, and ensuring all kids are covered. “Jeffries basically supported the first year of Medicare for All,” Sanders said. But anything that passes Congress the next two years will still need to be signed by President Donald Trump to take effect. Sanders rejected the notion that Trump, a Republican, wouldn't sign something like Medicare for All into law. "Donald Trump may be crazy, but he is not stupid. He’s a smart guy, and he’s a very good politician,” Sanders said. An agenda beyond healthcare Sanders is also preparing to use the committee to advance a broader economic agenda that includes raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $20 an hour and promoting the PRO Act, which would strengthen workers’ rights to unionize. The proposed wage increase would nearly triple the federal minimum, which has remained unchanged since 2009, and could face resistance from lawmakers concerned about the impact on small businesses and employment. Sanders proposes to implement it over a four-year transition period. Sanders’ agenda also calls for sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence , including a moratorium on new AI data centers , a pause in advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of Bernie Sanders at https://apnews.com/hub/bernie-sanders . This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/ap-exclusive-bernie-sanders-unveils-112846315.html

item.title: Iran attacks U.S. bases in Gulf countries despite diplomatic efforts to end 9-month war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Enas Alashray and Nayera Abdallah DUBAI, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Iran said it targeted US drone and missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the United States struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking Tehran's first attack on the US-allied Gulf state since September. Underlining a broader uptick in hostilities in recent days, Bahrain said ‌it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday for a third time in a week, accusing Tehran of a "systematic hostile approach" towards the Gulf kingdom, where the US Navy's Fifth ‌Fleet is headquartered. The latest attacks highlighted the obstacles facing diplomatic efforts to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices and drawn in countries across the region. IRAN ISSUES FRESH WARNING TO 'THE ENEMY' The ​Iranian army said it had targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base after Kuwait said its air defences were countering hostile drone attacks. It followed US airstrikes on Tuesday evening, when American fighter aircraft targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm in retaliation for Iranian attacks on US personnel and assets, a US military official told Reuters. Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack caused no damage to infrastructure. Kuwait said it reserved the right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and protect its territory and vital facilities against any aggression or threat. In videos published ‌by state media on Wednesday, Iranian Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami issued a ⁠fresh warning to the United States, which launched the war against Iran alongside Israel in February. "If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said. Hasan Al Hasan, a senior ⁠fellow for Middle East Policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said Iran was undertaking a "cautious" escalation. "But there is no ruling out further escalation, especially if the US begins to widen military operations, begins to widen its target set to include not just Iranian military coastal infrastructure, but also more deeply within Iran," he said. MEDIATOR QATAR AIMS TO NARROW GAPS The United States and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 and Tehran responded ​with ​strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. The conflict later spread to Lebanon, where fighting erupted ​between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah, and to Yemen, from where the Iran-aligned Houthis ‌have launched attacks on Saudi energy facilities, airports and other targets. Iran has also fired at US forces in Jordan. Global oil and gas prices have shot up with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted after Tehran declared it closed, while the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iran, hitting Iran's economy hard. Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said. A Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital Riyadh. There was no immediate confirmation from the Houthis. A surge in attacks on shipping since October has threatened to further strain global oil supplies. On Tuesday, a crew abandoned a liquefied petroleum gas ‌tanker off Oman's Khasab. The United Arab Emirates' ADNOC L&S said on Wednesday that one crew member was missing and ​11 injured after one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia condemned Iran's ​latest attacks. "The Kingdom renews its demand for an end to all acts of aggression, respect ​for international law and the principles of good neighborliness, and an opportunity for diplomatic efforts to achieve peace and resolve the crisis through negotiations," the ‌Saudi foreign ministry said. RUBIO SEES NO IMMINENT THREAT TO WASHINGTON Trump said on Tuesday ​the US was taking seriously the possibility that ​Iran could be planning an attack on Washington, when asked about a CNN report that cited US intelligence assessments on a potential Iranian plot involving a so-called dirty bomb. On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital. Iran's Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them "baseless." A dirty bomb uses conventional ​explosives to disperse radioactive material. Unlike a nuclear weapon, it does not ‌produce a nuclear explosion, but can spread radioactive contamination and cause significant disruption and public alarm. "I am not," Rubio said when asked by a reporter in Manila ​if he was concerned about an "imminent attack" on Washington. "I don't think there is any imminent threat." (Reporting by Enas Alashray in Cairo; Jana Choukeir and Elwely Elwelly in Dubai; ​Writing by Nayera Abdallah and Tom Perry, Editing by Stephen Coates, John Mair and Ros Russell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/bahrain-issues-clear-threat-alert-001609990.html

item.title: Report reveals that AI models could plan 'viable' terror attacks despite safeguards
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The world's leading artificial intelligence platforms were used to create "viable" plans to build homemade bombs and carry out mass casualty attacks in major U.S. cities in a test, according to a new government report released Wednesday. Using Claude, Grok, ChatGPT and Gemini, investigators with the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office produced "feasible information that could assist a malicious actor with planning and executing attacks" within 12 hours, using well-known techniques to bypass the platforms' guardrails, the agency wrote in its report. The report from the congressional watchdog comes at a time when breakthrough advances in AI have underscored the promise and potential of the rapidly evolving technology and raised new concerns by lawmakers in Washington about the potential for misuse. D3sign/Getty Images - PHOTO: Close up of hands typing on a computer keyboard. In recent years, gunmen have used A.I. to plan mass shootings in Florida and Canada, according to authorities. And one top A.I. company disclosed in September that users in Yemen unsuccessfully attempted to use its model to build missiles. "The same information that testers were able to get ahold of could be deadly in the hands of a terrorist who actually intends to carry out an attack," said Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who requested the study. Last April, researchers randomly assigned each of the platforms to one of two scenarios: an improvised explosive device (IED) attack, and an attack on the U.S. electrical grid. Two of the AI platforms generated distinct plots to build, deploy and execute IED attacks in major cities. They suggested specific dates, times and targets -- a hotel parking garage and a convention center -- around scheduled public events. Allison Robbert/AP Photo - PHOTO: Senate Treasury Investigators ran the experiment with each platform once, but randomized the tests and did not disclose which platforms produced each result. Both platforms suggested ways to avoid the attention of law enforcement; one produced a timeline for planning and executing the attack that recommended creating a shell company and purchasing supplies across multiple states. "At minimum [one] platform provided enough information that could help a malicious actor to avoid detection and produce a very large IED," the agency wrote in its report. Investigators verified the accuracy of the platforms' instructions with surveillance, research and by consulting a bomb squad commander at a "major metropolitan area" fire department. Open-source AI tool has been used to automate cyber intrusions: FBI The other two platforms provided instructions for targeting electrical grid substations in major U.S. cities, identifying specific drone and firearm models and how to acquire them. They also generated a map and image to help visualize the execution of the planned attacks. In statements to the GAO, Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), OpenAI (Chat GPT) and SpaceXAI (Grok), told the agency that they continually test their systems and update and expand safeguards built into their platforms, and have multiple layers of security to catch wrongdoing. All have taken steps since the study was conducted last spring to improve their models and safeguards, the companies told the GAO. "The companies also assure us that this is an area of concern and ongoing research," said Kevin Walsh, the director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO, told reporters. "However, we conclude that, in its current state, this technology can be dangerous, and its misuse represents a growing risk to our nation." The agency, which redacted specific results and model information from their tests and report to prevent misuse of their work, shared their findings with the artificial intelligence companies upon request. Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of 'catastrophic' risks The GAO also did not specify in its report if any of their experiments prompted a response from law enforcement but noted that some of the platforms suspended their accounts after the study was conducted. Hassan, the incoming chair of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee, said she plans to hold hearings on AI safety next year and work on new legislation to beef up safety requirements. "These companies are facing extraordinary competitive pressures to get their models out the door and to the public as quickly as possible," she said. "One of the things that will be necessary going forward to make sure that they're all dealing with the level playing field when it comes to safety, is making sure that before models are released, they have safeguards that can't be breached in this way." In a statement to ABC News, an OpenAI spokesperson said: "We take these findings seriously and appreciate the opportunity to work constructively with GAO, Senator Hassan and the relevant committees to address them. While the study findings are concerning, the testing took place months ago on an older version of ChatGPT, and we've made considerable safety improvements since then, including with our GPT-6 family of models. We rigorously test our safeguards internally and with external experts, and we use monitoring, human review and enforcement to identify and address misuse and strengthen our protections." ABC also reached out to Anthropic, Google and SpaceXAI. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/Technology/ai-models-plan-viable-attack-plots-test-despite/story?id=138229892

item.title: Peltola win doesn't end DOJ scrutiny of Alaska Senate race, officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the victor in Alaska’s Senate race Tuesday, but Justice Department officials say their interest in the contentious campaign has not waned. A criminal grand jury investigation remains underway into whether Peltola staffers or others recruited a spoiler candidate with a similar name to incumbent Dan S. Sullivan (R) in an effort to confuse voters - allegations Peltola has denied. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. In a parallel civil case, the Justice Department continues to appeal a federal judge’s ruling last month denying the agency’s extraordinary request to delay certification of the vote over concerns the outcome could be tainted by that potential effort to siphon efforts away from the incumbent. “The priority of investigating a criminal potential fraud doesn’t stop because of the election, no matter who wins or loses,” Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters last week. When asked whether his department would drop those legal battles if Peltola took a significant lead, Blanche added: “No. That investigation remains where it was, which means I’m not going to talk about it.” Still, after a flurry of activity on both legal fronts in the run-up to Election Day, there have been few public signs of progress since the Nov. 3 vote. After the race was called late Tuesday evening, a Justice Department spokesperson said the agency stands by Blanche’s earlier remarks. Peltola has denied any involvement in a scheme to confuse voters. The other Sullivan on the ballot - retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan - has repeatedly maintained his candidacy was legitimate. He ultimately netted fewer than 5,000 votes, less than half the more than 12,000-vote lead Peltola secured over her Republican opponent. Democrats have condemned both the civil suit and the criminal investigation as a norm-shattering effort by the Justice Department to influence the election’s outcome. Michael J. Heyman, the U.S. attorney in Alaska, took the unusual step of confirming the existence of the grand jury investigation, which had been underway since the summer, at a news conference five days before the election. Such probes are typically carried out in secret and Justice Department guidelines typically advise prosecutors from taking investigative steps before an election that could be seen as a sign of political bias. Though Heyman declined to discuss details of the probe, The Washington Post has reported that prosecutors have issued dozens of subpoenas and sent target letters and document preservation warnings to those it believes might have been involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan. Among the recipients was Marc Elias, a prominent Democratic voting rights and election lawyer, whose firm represented Peltola’s campaign. A lawyer at the firm, whose text messages were quoted in a New York Times story, documenting the alleged recruitment effort also received a target letter, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss details of the ongoing probe. Elias dismissed those warnings as the latest attempt by the Justice Department to target President Donald Trump’s political enemies. The Justice Department’s civil suit was filed just weeks before the vote and as early voting was underway. Department lawyers had asked the court to suspend certification, in the event of a narrow Republican loss, until an investigation could be carried out into whether the outcome had been tainted. In her Nov. 1 ruling dismissing the case, U.S. District Judge Sharon L. Gleason said she had no authority to order such a probe and noted the department had offered no suggestion as to how such an investigation could be carried out while respecting the secrecy of voters’ ballot choices. The department immediately appealed Gleason’s ruling to the San Francisco-based U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which has so far shown no sign of taking up the matter quickly. The court has set a briefing schedule for arguments that extends until Jan. 11 - more than a week after Peltola is expected to be sworn in. The Justice Department has not asked to accelerate that schedule or moved to withdraw its case. Richard L. Hasen, a prominent election law scholar at UCLA, urged the appellate judges not to let the matter linger in a “friend of the court” brief filed Friday. “This Court should send a swift and clear message to the federal government and the country,” Hasen wrote in the filing, “that the State of Alaska, and Alaska alone, has the right to certify the winner of its elections.” Patrick Marley contributed to this report. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/11/17/peltola-win-doesnt-end-doj-scrutiny-alaska-senate-race-officials-say/

item.title: White House pulls Trump's pick to lead FDA as Republican support falters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation. Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for President Donald Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary . But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his administration's approach to vaccines. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday morning. Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot — “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to disagree with Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic. But late Tuesday night, Cassidy suggested he had been prepared to back Overton and suggested her nomination was derailed by disagreements over abortion, not vaccines. “I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy stated in a posting on X. He went on to say that anti-abortion Republicans had sought commitments on “life issues” from the White House, but “the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.” Currently, the FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone — at the request of Trump — that could reinstate restrictions on the drug’s use, including a requirement for in-person prescribing. FDA has promised a report on its safety findings by March. To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on the chamber floor. Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January. It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee. Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee. Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton's approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children. Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides. Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists. “There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said. Trump has pulled back several other health nominations Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats. The FDA is currently being led on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency. The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org. item.title: Chinese President Xi rolls out the red carpet for Trump as a new trade fight looms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed President Trump with a rare in-person greeting Wednesday in Shenzhen for the Chinese leg of Trump's Asia trip this week. The Chinese leader even offered Trump a hug, kicking off a visit expected to be dogged by questions of US changes to semiconductor export controls and the ongoing scandal at Nvidia . Trade talks with China and Canada are also on the agenda. The greeting came ahead of two closely watched sit-down meetings Thursday between Trump and Xi on economic issues and another with Russian President Vladimir Putin joining the conversation. Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump upon his arrival at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 18 in Shenzhen, China. (Kevin Frayer/Getty Images) Kevin Frayer via Getty Images Trump landed in Shenzhen at 4:42 p.m. local time on Wednesday to a red carpet welcome ceremony, a military band playing the Star-Spangled Banner, and a military flyover, according to a pool report. The pomp mirrored Trump's tarmac greeting for Xi in the United States in September. Trump also met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum later on Wednesday. Carney posted on X that the leaders discussed efforts to reach a trade deal and "agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact." The meeting follows significant trade war escalations that erupted between the US and Canada earlier this fall. Recent weeks have seen a new round of talks aimed at reaching a deal to reduce current duties and avert a threatened 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts, scheduled to take effect in 2027. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney arrives for a press conference during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China on November 18. (WANG Zhao / POOL / AFP via Getty Images) WANG ZHAO via Getty Images In his own stops ahead of the meeting, Carney announced progress toward lessening trade restrictions with China and Mexico and also claimed that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is not a major concern for Trump. "We have been making progress," Carney said of talks with the US, but that any deal needs to be "in the interest of Canadians." Sheinbaum posted a photo of her sitting down with Trump and said it had been "a very good meeting." A day of opening ceremonies During Wednesday's whirlwind series of stops, Trump and Xi joined a group photo as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) fully kicked off. Trump crossed paths with Putin at the festivities, shaking hands and exchanging pleasantries with the Russian leader. The president then participated in a banquet before returning to his hotel for the night. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on on Wednesday. (Lori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images) IORI SAGISAWA via Getty Images The gathering this week had been set to focus on digital trade and artificial intelligence, but the scandal at Nvidia ( NVDA ) and potential changes to US semiconductor export rules are hanging over it. The Trump administration published new proposed export limits as Trump departed Washington, a move that was immediately felt in the region . The rule aims to limit China's ability to access advanced chips that reside in data centers outside its borders. It was authored by the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council and has now moved one step closer to being enacted. Trump traveled to China from the Philippines, where he participated in a series of economic meetings and signed a joint statement with Thailand as the two countries look to finalize a trade deal. This story has been updated with additional developments. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: Man with axe accused of destroying $60 million U.S. military plane in Ireland
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The $60m (£45m) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules was rendered inoperable and will not fly again, US prosecutors said. Photograph: US Department of Justice/PA An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks. O’Corrain is charged with destruction of US government property in connection with the incident in April at Shannon airport in the west of Ireland, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan. He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled, the AP news agency reported. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. The $60m (£45m) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules, which had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and will not fly again, US prosecutors said. O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged with causing criminal damage and trespassing. Manhattan US attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on US military assets – and thus our national security – will not be tolerated.” An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends said he disarmed the C-130 in protest against the US’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza. O’Corrain plotted the attack on 11 April for months, US prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking on to the airport’s grounds, prosecutors allege. O’Corrain subscribed to a phone app that provided live flight tracking and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, prosecutors added. He is also accused of trying to contact someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon airport, prosecutors said. O’Corrain breached the airport’s perimeter at about 4.40 am and broke into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said. The document added he used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and put ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said. James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said: “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/man-accused-destroying-us-military-000615511.html

item.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for next House speaker
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nolan D. McCaskill WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Democrats elected this month to the US House of Representatives nominated Hakeem Jeffries ‌on Wednesday to lead them in the next Congress, putting ‌him on the precipice of becoming the nation's first Black House speaker. The incoming House ​Democratic Caucus nominated Jeffries in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote. Jeffries won 251 votes with 11 Democrats opposing him. Many incoming progressives declined to say whether they would back Jeffries after the November 3 midterm elections, with several saying ‌they wanted a leader ⁠who would support a bold agenda to pass populist policies that candidates campaigned on. A group of seven incoming ⁠House progressives said in a joint statement that they voted against Jeffries because they're still working to secure commitments from the New York Democrat. "While we ​have ​seen meaningful progress, there is still ​work to be done to ‌ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership," they said. "Those conversations are ongoing." Despite some opposition, Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the presidency, when the new ‌Congress convenes in early January. The speaker ​election requires 218 votes on the House ​floor. Democrats will have a ​majority of at least 257 seats. Several competitive ‌races remain uncalled. House Republicans last week ​nominated Judiciary Committee ​Chairman Jim Jordan to lead their conference in January. Jordan won the post over Majority Leader Steve Scalise after Speaker Mike Johnson ​said he would ‌not seek to lead Republicans in the minority. (Reporting by Nolan ​D. McCaskill; Additional reporting by David Morgan, Richard Cowan and ​Katharine Jackson; Editing by Nick Zieminski) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/democrats-nominate-hakeem-jeffries-next-153612207.html

item.title: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous people in Brazil raises fears for their safety
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — A rare encounter between Indigenous people living in isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest and members of a neighboring community has prompted government protections amid concerns about the group’s health and threats to its forest home. The encounter began Monday near a government access control post and the Guajajara Indigenous village of Tawari in the northeastern state of Maranhao, according to a statement Tuesday from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples. The ministry said around 20 members of the isolated Awa people had been sighted approaching the area in the Arariboia Indigenous Territory, but cautioned that information remained preliminary as authorities assessed the situation. The encounter has raised concerns about why members of a group that has spent decades hunting, fishing and gathering food while avoiding outsiders would suddenly approach a neighboring community, particularly as illegal logging, hunting and other intrusions threaten their forest territory. Images of the encounter have also drawn widespread attention. Sarah Shenker, head of Survival Brasil, part of Survival International, an organization that advocates for Indigenous peoples’ rights, called the encounter “a crisis moment really and a wake-up call,” urging Brazilian authorities to crack down on illegal intrusions into Awa territory. She said the images could help reinforce the existence of isolated Indigenous groups, whose presence is sometimes disputed by those seeking access to their lands. But she warned that the circumstances surrounding the encounter were troubling. An unusual encounter with the isolated Awa people documented Footage recorded by members of the neighboring Guajajara Indigenous community and shared by Survival International shows Awa adults and children gathered amid dense vegetation, some carrying bows and arrows and wearing feathered headdresses and necklaces. The reason for the group’s approach remains unclear, but Survival International says the Awa apparently approached a government team, asked for yams and took them back into the forest. The Arariboia territory has faced decades of pressure from illegal intruders, Shenker said, leaving isolated communities increasingly vulnerable as surrounding forests have been cleared. The Brazilian government said the Awa group is already registered in the official database of isolated Indigenous peoples and is monitored by a specialized protection team from Funai, the federal Indigenous affairs agency. Funai personnel and Indigenous health workers are now in the area, and authorities have activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess potential contact situations and health risks. Survival International has previously estimated that around 100 Awa remain uncontacted, although that is not necessarily a current population count. Other Awa live in settled villages and maintain contact with outsiders. Fears for the tribe's safety One of the most immediate concerns is the risk of disease. Indigenous peoples living in isolation can be particularly vulnerable to infectious illnesses because of their limited previous exposure to pathogens common in the wider population. The ministry stressed that its policy is not to encourage contact, but to protect the Awa’s right to remain isolated and determine for themselves whether to establish relations with outsiders. It also cautioned that a brief encounter does not necessarily mean a group has abandoned its isolation or chosen to establish permanent contact. The Arariboia territory is also home to the Guajajara people, whose Indigenous forest guardians have spent years monitoring their lands and confronting illegal intrusions. Shenker said those efforts have led to violence against the community, including killings of some community members, while responsibility for protecting the territory ultimately rests with the Brazilian government. “The only way that they will survive is if intruders are kept out of their forest once and for all,” she said. Despite the attention generated by the rare images, Shenker said she would rather the Awa had remained out of sight, living undisturbed in their forest. “We would rather not have images and not have video footage of the uncontacted Awa when that means that they are living in the way that they choose in their forest, able to get on with their lives, hunting, fishing, gathering,” she said. ___ Reporter Gabriela Sá Pessoa in Sao Paulo, Brazil, contributed to this report. ___ The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. item.title: Mullin faces congressional hearing in the wake of historic nationwide ground stop
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is on Capitol Hill on Wednesday to talk about worldwide threats since Sept. 11, 2001, but he's likely to be in the hot seat over questions about technology issues that disrupted millions of Americans over the last week. Mullin is testifying before the House Committee on Homeland Security for a hearing underway titled "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" along with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images - PHOTO: Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin arrives to testify during a House Committee on Homeland Security hearing on Capitol Hill, November 18, 2026 in Washington. Mullin is expected to be grilled over the investigation into last Friday's rare nationwide ground stop , the second since 9/11. This ground stop stranded millions of passengers going into last weekend. He is also expected to receive questions about the cyber outages that have affected airlines, Microsoft Outlook, banks and other services. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton speak with each other before the start of a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, November 18, 2026. Mullin has repeatedly assured the public that Friday's air traffic incident, in which flights were grounded for four hours, was not nefarious and echoed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on what caused the disruption. Duffy told ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that work was being performed to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred. Timeline of the FAA nationwide ground stop: How it developed The ground stop was issued after the installation of a Juniper router at the Arkansas facility flooded the network with data, overwhelming an older system and resulting in telecommunications issues, according to officials. Duffy told reporters on Tuesday that the FAA had spent a year testing the routers and that the issue occurred on the 69th installation. Open-source AI tool has been used to automate cyber intrusions: FBI Mullin told CNBC in an interview on Tuesday that "the FAA issue was because they're working on 50-year-old equipment with copper wire, that should be fiber." He also stressed that the U.S. is not under attack. "There's no cyber threat that's taking place. The homeland is very secure," he said. Mullin could also face questions about his trip to Louisiana on Saturday to attend the Texas-LSU college football game while thousands of flights were still disrupted from the ground stop the day before. The secretary told CNBC he would not have flown if the airways weren't open. "And we still got to live our life at the same time," he added. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/Politics/mullin-faces-congressional-hearing-wake-historic-nationwide-ground/story?id=138226960
